title: Long answers and the rollout queue: what an over-provisioned fleet costs
design_ref: Long trajectories and the long tail
purpose: Compare the same recipe with a rollout queue sized to the trainer and with one sized to the fleet, with and without asynchrony, and with a mode that makes answers ten times longer.

steps.display: kubectl -n rl-scale get lws rollout   # 2 engine(s), settings: defaults
aws s3 cp s3://<state bucket>/runs/r1-center/metrics.jsonl -   # the run 'queue sized to the trainer (64 rollouts in flight)' made earlier in this session
# run q512: read back from the state bucket (already complete)
# run sync0: read back from the state bucket (already complete)
python compare.py r1-center q512 sync0   # 40 steps of the same recipe, three ways of running it
steps.output:

steps.display: kubectl -n rl-scale exec rollout-0 -- curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep cache_config_info   # how many long answers fit on one engine
steps.output: 15960 blocks of 16 tokens = 255,360 tokens of KV cache; the engine reports a maximum concurrency of 31.2 requests at the full length of 4096 tokens

checks.description: a queue sized to the fleet throws away far more samples than one sized to the trainer
checks.because: The trainer uses a few dozen samples a step. A fleet allowed 512 rollouts in flight generates thousands, and a sample older than the staleness bound is dropped when the trainer reaches it. Those tokens were generated for nothing.

checks.description: the over-sized queue stalls the weight sync: a pause of more than 20 seconds appears, and never with the sized one
checks.because: The trainer asks the fleet to pause, and the request waits behind the work already in flight. With a shorter queue there is little to wait for.

checks.description: the over-sized queue costs more GPU hours to reach the same step
checks.because: GPU hours are the three reserved GPUs times the run's time, with the evaluation left out.

checks.description: without asynchrony each step takes longer: generation and training no longer overlap
checks.because: With a staleness bound of 0 the rollouts for step n+1 start only after the weights of step n have loaded. The trainer then waits for the first groups.

checks.description: thinking mode makes answers several times longer
checks.because: The same model and prompts, with its reasoning turned on. Every group of answers now takes seconds, not a fraction of one.

checks.description: the longest answers hit the limit, and a large share is cut
checks.because: An answer cut at the limit is a failed answer to the reward function. How such answers are counted (masked or penalised) is a Design 06 choice that interacts with the budget.

checks.description: the trainer now waits for rollouts for a visible share of its time, which it did not with short answers
checks.because: With short answers the fleet runs ahead of the trainer and the asynchrony hides the generation time. With answers of thousands of tokens the slowest group of a step decides when the trainer can go on: the long tail.
